name: Linkedinmaxxing

card.summary: Optimising a LinkedIn profile and profile photo so you present as a polished, high-status professional and get more career opportunities.

quick.overview:
Linkedinmaxxing is the practice of tuning every part of a LinkedIn profile (photo, headline, work history, endorsements, verification) so that the person looks credible, successful and attractive to recruiters and contacts. The appearance payoff is mostly about the profile photo: a well-lit, well-groomed headshot is the first thing viewers see.

The term is a looksmaxxing-style coinage that applies the idea of maximising a single trait to career presentation. It is discussed in a few looksmax.org threads, where users say it has helped them professionally; no formal research tests the label itself.
quick.how: Practitioners typically update the profile photo with good lighting, grooming and clothing, sometimes hiring a photographer, and complete the profile fields the platform prompts for, such as work experience, skills and verification badges.
quick.risks: The practice carries little physical risk. Commonly mentioned downsides are time and the cost of professional photography; a heavily edited photo can also differ from how someone looks in person.

lead: Linkedinmaxxing is a looksmaxxing-adjacent term for optimising a LinkedIn profile, especially the photo, so that the person comes across as polished and high-status in a professional setting. It applies the maxxing idea (improving one feature as far as possible) to career presentation rather than to the face or body.[1]

LinkedIn profiles typically show work experience, education, skills and a personal photo, and members can add verification badges and receive endorsements.[2] People who practise linkedinmaxxing treat these elements as a package and refine them together. A looksmax.org user in one thread says their heavily refined profile has been responsible for much of their success at work.[1]
No published study has tested linkedinmaxxing as such. The platform's own description of profile features does not cite research on photo effects.[2]

chain: Stronger first impression on recruiters and contacts
angle.text: Practitioners use a high-quality headshot and a complete profile to make a stronger first impression in professional networking. Users in looksmaxxing forums say this has helped their careers.[1]

paras: The practice centres on the profile photo, the headline and summary, the work history, and platform features such as skills endorsements and verification badges.[2] Wikipedia notes that some members hire professional photographers for their profile photos and quotes a consultant who calls having no photo the most common profile mistake; this is an opinion, not a study.[2]

On looksmax.org the topic appears in threads asking whether it is worthwhile. One reply says their profile is optimised heavily and is responsible for a lot of success at their job.[1] The wording is jokey and anecdotal, in the style of forum rating slang.

lore.intro: Discussion is limited to a small number of forum posts treating the profile as another feature to maximise.[1]

claims.claim: A maxxed LinkedIn profile drives career success
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user says their profile is highly optimised and responsible for much of their success at work.[1]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined linkedinmaxxing as a practice.
